title: WHAT IF THE DEVIL ISN’T ATTACKING YOU… WHAT IF GOD IS CONFRONTING YOU?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE DEVIL ISN’T ATTACKING YOU… WHAT IF GOD IS CONFRONTING YOU?

We have become so quick to rebuke the enemy that sometimes we refuse to recognize our own responsibility. But what if the very thing you keep calling spiritual warfare is actually the mercy of God exposing what you have been unwilling to change?
There is a kind of prayer that sounds spiritual but can hide a dangerous refusal to take responsibility.
“Lord, the enemy is attacking my marriage.”
“Lord, Satan is destroying my relationships.”
“Lord, the devil is blocking my blessings.”
“Lord, people are coming against me because of my calling.”
And sometimes, those prayers come from a place of genuine spiritual warfare.

Scripture does not deny the existence of Satan. Jesus Himself was tempted by the devil in the wilderness. Peter warned believers to remain watchful because their adversary prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). Paul reminded the church that our struggle is not ultimately against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).
Spiritual warfare is real.
What if the enemy you keep rebuking is not the reason your life keeps falling apart?
What if your marriage is struggling because you have stopped listening?
What if your friendships keep ending because you refuse correction?
What if your finances are suffering because you keep making decisions without wisdom or restraint?
What if the peace you are praying for cannot grow because you keep returning to the very behavior that destroys it?
And what if the people you have labeled enemies are sometimes the very people God has allowed to speak a truth you desperately need to hear?
Read that again.
Because not every uncomfortable conversation is persecution.
Not every closed door is demonic opposition.
Not every consequence is a curse.
And not everyone who confronts you is being used by Satan.
Sometimes the most dangerous thing standing between you and spiritual growth is not an invisible enemy.
Sometimes it is the version of yourself that refuses to be corrected.
And if that sentence stings, please do not leave yet.
Because this is not a story about how terrible you are.
It is about how deeply Jesus loves people He refuses to leave unchanged.
Imagine a man sitting alone in his car outside his house.
The engine is off. The street is quiet. His phone is resting beside him.
Another argument with his wife.
Another evening ending in silence.
Another message from someone he loves saying, “I cannot keep doing this.”
He closes his eyes and whispers, “God, why is the enemy attacking my family?”
And he means it.
He loves God. He attends church. He listens to sermons. He knows how to pray.
But he also knows something else.
He knows how sharply he speaks when he is angry.
He knows how quickly he becomes defensive when his wife expresses pain.
He knows how often he apologizes without actually changing.
He knows that whenever someone confronts him, he finds a way to make himself the victim.
Yet somehow, in every prayer, the devil gets blamed for the damage his own words have caused.
Then, in the quiet of that car, a painful thought crosses his mind.
“What if I have been asking God to remove an attack when I should have been asking Him to change my heart?”
No thunder.
No dramatic vision.
Just a man finally becoming willing to tell the truth.
That is where repentance can begin.
And perhaps someone reading this is closer to that moment than they want to admit.
Because it is possible to love the language of spiritual warfare while avoiding the discipline of spiritual maturity.
It is possible to quote Scripture while refusing to obey the very Scripture we quote.
It is possible to pray against pride in other people while protecting pride in ourselves.
And it is possible to become so convinced that everyone is against us that we stop asking whether anyone might actually be trying to help us.
The Bible gives us a sobering example.
King David was not an unbeliever. He was not a stranger to God's presence. He was a man who had experienced extraordinary victories, divine deliverance, and the mercy of the Lord.
Yet David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged for her husband Uriah to be killed.
You can read the account in 2 Samuel 11.
For a time, David continued living as king.
He still had authority.
He still had a throne.
He still possessed the outward appearance of someone blessed by God.
But something was terribly wrong beneath the royal garments.
Then God sent the prophet Nathan.
Nathan told David a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb.
David became furious.
He could clearly recognize injustice when someone else was responsible for it.
But he could not yet see the injustice in himself.
And then Nathan spoke four devastating words.
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7, KJV
Imagine the silence.
The king who could identify another man's sin was suddenly forced to confront his own.
David could have accused Nathan of rebellion.
He could have called the confrontation a spiritual attack.
He could have used his position to silence the prophet.
He could have declared that anyone questioning God's anointed king was opposing God Himself.
But David did something different.
He confessed.
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
There was no elaborate defense.
No attempt to blame Bathsheba.
No accusation against Nathan.
No convenient explanation about the pressures of leadership.
Just the truth.
And in that confession, we see something that our generation desperately needs to recover.
Accountability is not always an attack on your calling. Sometimes it is God's mercy protecting you from what your uncorrected character could destroy.
But notice something equally important.
David's confession did not erase every earthly consequence of his actions.
God forgave David, yet the consequences of his sin remained deeply painful.
That distinction matters.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
Restoration is real.
But grace is not permission to pretend that our decisions have no consequences.
In Psalm 51, David gives us one of Scripture's most profound prayers of repentance.
He cries:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
The Hebrew expression translated “create in me” is בְּרָא־לִי (berāʾ-lî), from the verb בָּרָא (bārāʾ), meaning “to create.”
It is the same Hebrew verb used in Genesis 1:1 when Scripture declares that God created the heavens and the earth.
That connection is extraordinary.
David was not merely asking God to improve his public image.
He was pleading for an inward work that only God could accomplish.
The word translated “clean” is טָהוֹר (ṭāhôr), carrying the sense of purity or cleanness.
And the Hebrew word for heart, לֵב (lēb), encompasses the inner person, including thought, desire, and will.
David was asking for something deeper than relief from embarrassment.
He wanted a heart made clean before God.
Not merely a reputation repaired before people.
Not merely consequences removed.
Not merely the discomfort of conviction silenced.
He wanted transformation.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been avoiding.
Because we would rather pray, “Lord, expose my enemies,” than “Lord, expose what is wrong in me.”
We would rather ask God to vindicate our behavior than surrender our behavior to His judgment.
We want victory without examination.
Deliverance without repentance.
Restoration without responsibility.
But Jesus never promised that following Him would mean never being confronted.
In fact, He taught something radically different.
In Matthew 7:3–5, Jesus describes a person who notices a speck in someone else's eye while ignoring a beam in their own.
Think about that picture.
Someone attempting delicate eye surgery while a massive piece of wood obstructs their own vision.
It is almost absurd.
And that is precisely the point.
Jesus was exposing the hypocrisy of people who become experts in identifying everyone else's failures while remaining strangely blind to their own.
The Greek word translated “hypocrite” in Matthew 7:5 is ὑποκριτά (hypokrita), a form of ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs).
In this context, it identifies someone whose outward judgment of another is contradicted by their own unaddressed sin.
Jesus did not tell His followers to ignore every problem in other people.
He told them to deal with their own obstruction first so they could see clearly enough to help.
That is not condemnation.
That is a call to humility.
And humility is difficult when we have built our entire identity around always being the wounded one, the misunderstood one, the betrayed one, the person everyone else has supposedly wronged.
There are people who have genuinely been betrayed.
There are believers who have endured abuse, manipulation, rejection, persecution, and injustice.
Their suffering must never be dismissed.
Accountability does not mean blaming victims for what others did to them.
And no one should be pressured to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation simply to prove that they are humble, forgiving, or spiritually mature.
But there is another reality we must confront.
Sometimes we are not only the people who have been hurt.
Sometimes we have also hurt others.
Sometimes we are not only the ones who need healing.
We are the ones who need to repent.
And both truths can exist in the same person.
You can have wounds that deserve compassion and habits that require correction.
You can have experienced betrayal and still be responsible for the way you treat others.
You can need God's comfort and God's conviction at the same time.
One does not cancel the other.
Consider Peter.
Peter loved Jesus.
He was passionate, outspoken, courageous at moments, and fiercely confident in his loyalty.
When Jesus warned that His disciples would stumble, Peter insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he would not.
Yet before the rooster crowed, Peter denied knowing Jesus three times.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The man who had confidently declared his loyalty suddenly realized the depth of his failure.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Jesus did not need to invent a false accusation to humble Peter.
Peter's own actions exposed the gap between his confidence and his character.
But the story did not end beside that fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
The conversation was painful.
Personal.
Restorative.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never failed.
Neither did He declare that Peter's failure made him forever useless.
Instead, Jesus recommissioned him to care for His sheep.
That is the beauty of Gospel restoration.
Jesus does not heal us by denying what happened. He heals us through truth, grace, and a restored relationship with Him.
Some of us want the restoration of Peter without the honesty of Peter.
We want Jesus to entrust us with greater responsibility while we refuse to acknowledge how we mishandled the responsibility we already had.
We want the next door opened without examining why the last one closed.
We want new relationships while repeating the patterns that wounded the old ones.
We want a fresh beginning without surrendering the behaviors that made the previous season so destructive.
But what if the greatest miracle God wants to work in your life right now is not changing everyone around you?
What if it is changing you?
Not because everyone else is innocent.
Not because your suffering is imaginary.
Not because the enemy is never active.
But because the Holy Spirit is deeply concerned with the condition of your heart.
James 1:14 teaches:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.” — KJV
James is not denying spiritual opposition.
He is reminding believers that sinful desire within the human heart also matters.
We cannot blame every sinful decision on the devil.
The enemy may tempt.
The world may pressure.
Our flesh may desire.
But we are still called to resist temptation, confess sin, and walk in obedience.
James 4:7 says:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — KJV
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
We sometimes emphasize the second command while neglecting the first.
We want authority to resist darkness while resisting God's authority over our own decisions.
We want to rebuke the enemy while refusing to surrender our bitterness.
We want to cast out fear while feeding our minds with deception.
We want to defeat division while spreading gossip.
We want the protection of truth while continuing to lie.
But spiritual warfare cannot become a substitute for spiritual obedience.
You cannot repent on behalf of someone else.
You cannot blame your way into holiness.
And you cannot rebuke away a pattern of behavior you are determined to keep practicing.
The apostle Paul makes this deeply practical.
Ephesians 4 calls believers to put away falsehood, speak truthfully, deal with anger without sinning, stop stealing, work honestly, abandon corrupt speech, and forgive one another.
These are not glamorous instructions.
They do not always produce dramatic testimonies.
They rarely look impressive on a stage.
But they reveal what transformed lives actually look like.
A husband who learns to listen.
A wife who chooses truth instead of manipulation.
A parent who apologizes to a child.
A pastor who welcomes appropriate accountability rather than hiding behind spiritual authority.
A ministry leader who handles money transparently.
A Christian who stops spreading rumors disguised as prayer requests.
A believer who finally says, “I was wrong, and I need to make this right.”
That is not weakness.
That is evidence of the Spirit's work.
Proverbs 12:1 says:
“Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.” — KJV
The Hebrew word translated “reproof” is תּוֹכַחַת (tôkhaḥat), which refers to correction, rebuke, or reproof.
Biblical wisdom does not treat all correction as hostility.
It recognizes that truthful correction can protect us from foolishness.
Of course, not everyone who criticizes you is correct.
Some criticism is unfair.
Some correction is abusive.
Some accusations are false.
Some people use the language of accountability to control others.
That is why discernment matters.
Biblical accountability must be rooted in truth, humility, love, and justice.
Galatians 6:1 tells spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in wrongdoing with gentleness, while remaining watchful over themselves.
The Greek word translated “restore” is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from καταρτίζω (katartizō), meaning to restore, put in order, or make fit.
The goal is not humiliation.
It is restoration.
Not public destruction.
Not superiority.
Not revenge disguised as righteousness.
Restoration.
And that means accountability is not a weapon we use to crush people.
It is a responsibility we exercise with humility, care, and reverence for God.
When correction is genuine, we should examine it rather than automatically reject it.
When accusations are false, we can respond truthfully without surrendering to bitterness.
When harm has occurred, repentance may require restitution, changed behavior, appropriate boundaries, and the patient rebuilding of trust.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
And reconciliation does not always mean returning to the same relationship or situation.
Grace never requires us to abandon wisdom.
Now consider something even more uncomfortable.
Have you ever noticed how quickly we can identify spiritual attacks when our own comfort is threatened?
Someone challenges our behavior.
“That's the enemy trying to discourage me.”
Someone questions our decision.
“That's Satan trying to block my purpose.”
Someone asks us to explain how we handled money, leadership, or responsibility.
“That's persecution against God's work.”
But what if the question is legitimate?
What if the concern is justified?
What if the person speaking is not trying to destroy you but trying to prevent greater damage?
We must be especially careful when spiritual language becomes a shield against examination.
No pastor is above accountability.
No ministry is above accountability.
No Christian influencer is above accountability.
No spiritual gift, testimony, title, or following places a person beyond the authority of God's Word.
Even the apostle Peter was publicly confronted by Paul when his conduct contradicted the truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
Peter was an apostle.
Yet his position did not make his behavior untouchable.
And Paul's confrontation was not evidence that Paul hated Peter.
It was a necessary defense of Gospel truth.
If an apostle could be corrected, why do some of us behave as though correction is an insult to our anointing?
Maybe because accountability threatens the image we have worked so hard to protect.
We want people to see our faith.
Our strength.
Our sacrifice.
Our spiritual maturity.
But we are afraid they might discover our inconsistency.
And so we hide.
We explain.
We deflect.
We blame.
We spiritualize.
We create elaborate stories about enemies and attacks because the simple truth feels unbearable.
“I was selfish.”
“I lied.”
“I was careless.”
“I became proud.”
“I hurt someone who trusted me.”
“I need help.”
“I need to change.”
Those sentences may be difficult to say.
But they can become the beginning of freedom.
Because the Gospel does not require you to maintain a flawless image.
It calls you to come honestly to a flawless Savior.
First John 1:8–9 says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
The Greek verb translated “confess” in verse 9 is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from ὁμολογέω (homologeō), meaning to confess, acknowledge, or admit.
The word carries the idea of openly acknowledging what is true.
In this passage, confession means honestly acknowledging our sins before God rather than denying them.
And look at the promise.
God is faithful and just to forgive.
He cleanses.
He does not invite us to confess so He can enjoy humiliating us.
He invites us into the light because darkness cannot give us the fellowship, forgiveness, and cleansing we need.
This is where everything changes.
Because Christianity is not a religion of people pretending they have never fallen.
It is the good news of Jesus Christ saving sinners who cannot save themselves.
At the cross, Jesus bore our sins.
He did not excuse evil.
He did not declare rebellion harmless.
He did not redefine sin so that nobody would feel uncomfortable.
He took sin seriously enough to give His life for sinners.
And He loved sinners deeply enough to do it willingly.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
Not while we were already perfect.
Not after we had repaired every relationship.
Not once we had learned to behave respectably.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is why repentance is not hopelessness.
That is why confession does not have to become self-destruction.
That is why accountability, rightly practiced, can become part of a believer's journey toward healing.
Because the same Jesus who exposes sin offers forgiveness to the repentant.
The same Savior who calls us to deny ourselves also promises His presence as we follow Him.
The same Lord who confronted Peter restored him.
The same God who heard David's confession remains merciful to sinners who turn to Him.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Grace is not God agreeing to leave us enslaved to the sins that are destroying us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And sometimes the training of grace feels uncomfortable because it challenges something we have been defending for years.
Maybe your anger.
Maybe your dishonesty.
Maybe your jealousy.
Maybe your secret addiction.
Maybe your habit of blaming everyone else.
Maybe the way you treat your spouse behind closed doors.
Maybe the way you handle criticism.
Maybe your refusal to seek help because admitting a problem feels like admitting defeat.
But seeking help is not defeat.
Confessing sin is not defeat.
Making restitution is not defeat.
Learning to listen is not defeat.
Taking responsibility is not defeat.
Sometimes the first visible evidence that pride is losing its grip is a person finally becoming willing to say:
“I need to change.”
And perhaps the most powerful prayer you can pray tonight is not, “God, fight everyone who is against me.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, show me where I am wrong.”
“Show me what I have been refusing to see.”
“Show me whom I have hurt.”
“Show me where I have confused conviction with condemnation.”
“Show me where I need boundaries and where I need repentance.”
“Give me courage to receive truthful correction.”
“And teach me to stop using spiritual language to avoid spiritual growth.”
That prayer takes courage.
Because God may bring something to your attention that requires an apology.
He may convict you about a habit you have justified.
He may lead you to seek wise counsel.
He may show you that a relationship needs repair.
He may also reveal that you have accepted blame for harm that was never yours to carry.
True accountability is not automatic self-condemnation.
It is an honest willingness to bring the facts, our actions, and our motives into the light of God's truth.
And sometimes, that truth brings both correction and comfort.
There is a beautiful distinction in 2 Corinthians 7:10:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” — KJV
The Greek word for repentance here is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It refers to repentance, a genuine turning of heart and mind that bears fruit in changed conduct.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
It is not performing tears so people will stop asking questions.
It is not apologizing only because consequences have arrived.
It is a genuine turning toward God that becomes visible in how we live.
A person can cry and remain unrepentant.
A person can feel embarrassed and remain unchanged.
A person can quote a hundred verses and still refuse responsibility.
But when the grace of Christ produces genuine repentance, the direction of a life begins to change.
Not instant perfection.
Not a flawless record.
But a real turning.
A willingness to make things right where possible.
A willingness to learn.
A willingness to be corrected again.
A willingness to walk in the light even when the light reveals something painful.
And that brings us to the question I want you to carry long after this article disappears from your screen.
Are you fighting a spiritual attack, or are you fighting the accountability that could help you grow?
Do not answer too quickly.
Sometimes it really is spiritual warfare.
Sometimes it is the consequences of our choices.
Sometimes it is injustice committed against us.
Sometimes it is a mixture of spiritual struggle, human weakness, relational conflict, and painful circumstances.
Not every hardship has one simple explanation.
That is why we need Scripture, prayer, discernment, honest self-examination, and trustworthy counsel.
But whatever the cause, we should never become so committed to proving that we are under attack that we refuse to ask whether God is calling us to repent.
Because the goal of following Jesus is not to win every argument about who was wrong.
The goal is to become more like Christ.
And Jesus Christ, though sinless, humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:5 calls believers to have the mind of Christ.
The One who had every right to glory took the form of a servant.
The One who was truly righteous never needed to manufacture righteousness through excuses.
The One who could have called legions of angels endured the cross to accomplish our redemption.
If our Savior embraced humility, how can we defend our pride as though it were a spiritual gift?
If our Savior spoke truth, how can we keep building our lives around excuses?
If our Savior gave Himself for us, how can we keep refusing the surrender He calls us to?
Maybe tonight, someone needs to stop composing another message explaining why everyone else is wrong.
Maybe someone needs to call their spouse and listen without interrupting.
Maybe a parent needs to sit beside a child and say, “I should not have spoken to you that way. Will you forgive me?”
Maybe a ministry leader needs to welcome honest questions rather than punish those who ask them.
Maybe a friend needs to admit that the relationship did not end only because the other person was difficult.
Maybe someone who has been mistreated needs to stop accepting false guilt and seek safety, support, and healing.
And maybe someone who has spent years calling every confrontation an attack needs to recognize that truth can be painful without being an enemy.
I do not know which of those stories resembles yours.
But I know this.
Jesus is not asking you to save yourself by becoming better.
He is calling you to come to Him in repentance and faith, receive His grace, and follow Him into a transformed life.
Your past does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your worst decision does not have to become the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to be the end of your story.
But neither does your pain give you permission to keep hurting others.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
At the empty tomb, hope rises.
And in the life of a repentant believer, the Gospel continues to bear fruit.
Not that Jesus makes every consequence disappear.
Not that every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
Not that repentance earns salvation.
But that through His death and resurrection, sinners can receive forgiveness, be reconciled to God, and begin walking in newness of life.
And that transformation is not merely a beautiful idea.
It reaches into our homes.
Our conversations.
Our finances.
Our habits.
Our relationships.
Our private decisions.
Our public responsibilities.
Even the way we respond when someone tells us we are wrong.
Before you leave, I want to ask something personal.
What is one area of your life where God may be calling you to take responsibility instead of making another excuse?
You do not have to expose private details or confess something publicly that belongs in a safe, appropriate conversation.
There is no shame in asking for prayer.
You may be surprised how many people are quietly wrestling with the same questions.
And if this article reminded you of someone you love, consider sharing it with them gently, not as a weapon or an accusation, but as an invitation to seek Christ together.
Not because every friend needs to be corrected by you.
But because every one of us needs the Gospel, and someone in your circle may be waiting for a reminder that Jesus offers both truth and grace.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow along.
Because our mission is not to create people who merely know how to sound Christian.
It is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ, who saves, forgives, restores, and transforms.
And if this ministry has been spiritually nourishing you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand the reach of Christ-centered articles, Scripture teaching, discipleship materials, and resources that encourage people to grow in biblical truth.

We want those resources and the message of the Gospel to continue reaching people who may never walk into a church building, who may be silently struggling, or who may be only one honest encounter with Scripture away from beginning to seek Jesus.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, faithful stewardship, and generous giving according to your means and convictions.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not fear.
Not guilt.
These items can serve as everyday reminders of faith, encouragement, and the message of Christ.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a ministry committed to making Jesus known and helping people grow in His Word.
Others will share, pray, encourage, and participate in the conversations.
Every form of sincere support is appreciated.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
And the invitation to repent, believe, and follow Him remains open regardless of anyone's ability to give.
Now, before you go, return to the question that started all of this.
What if the devil is not behind every difficult thing happening in your life?
What if some of the discomfort you feel is the result of truth finally reaching a place you have kept hidden?
What if God is inviting you to stop defending the old version of yourself and begin surrendering more fully to Christ?
You do not need another excuse to remain unchanged.
You need the Savior who died and rose again to redeem you.
And if He is showing you something that needs to change, do not run from the light.
Bring it to Him.
Confess what is yours to confess.
Reject the guilt that is not yours to carry.
Receive His forgiveness.
Make things right where you can.
Seek help where you need it.
And keep following Jesus.
Because the most dangerous prison is not always the one built by your enemies.
Sometimes it is the one built by the excuses you refuse to surrender.
And the moment you stop defending what is destroying you may be the moment you finally begin to experience the freedom Christ has been calling you into.
